opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the open-source community has changed a lot over the past few years, especially in AI.

A few years ago, open source in machine learning was mostly about frameworks and research code. People released a paper with a GitHub repo, and maybe some model weights, but the most capable systems were mostly closed. What's changed is that open-weight models have become strong enough that people can build real products on them. When high-quality open models started coming out, from Llama to Mistral to DeepSeek and Qwen, the whole ecosystem took off. Suddenly a lot of people needed to run, fine-tune, and serve these models efficiently, and that created demand for open infrastructure.

From my own experience working on inference systems like SGLang, and earlier on projects around serving and efficiency, the biggest change is the speed. Something gets released and within days, sometimes hours, the community has support for it, optimized kernels, quantized versions, benchmarks. That pace of iteration is something no single company could match. The community has also become much more international. Some of the most important contributions now come from teams in China, Europe, and many universities, not only a few big labs in the Bay Area.

Another change is that open source has become more professionalized. It used to be mostly individuals and academic groups doing it for passion or research credit. Now companies contribute engineers full time, startups are built around open-source projects, and there's real collaboration between academia and industry. That brings more resources and stability, but it also raises questions about governance, sustainability, and who sets the direction.

I'm quite optimistic overall. Open source helps make sure that cutting-edge AI isn't controlled by just a handful of organizations. It lowers the barrier for researchers and developers, and it builds transparency and trust. There are still challenges, like the gap with the very best closed models at the frontier, the compute cost of training, and maintainer burnout. But I think the community is healthier and more impactful now than at any point I've seen.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes open source becoming more professionalized and raises governance and sustainability questions, but does not say opportunistic participation weakens existing believers’ confidence.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions companies and startups contributing to open source, but does not say this makes it harder to distinguish genuine commitment from instrumental motives.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest change is that open source in AI stopped being a side activity and became the main battlefield. A few years ago, if you wanted to work on a state-of-the-art model, you basically had to be inside one of a handful of labs. The weights were closed, the training recipes were closed, and the community mostly worked on tooling around the edges.

That shifted pretty dramatically. First with the Llama releases, then with a wave of strong open models coming out of a lot of different places, including a lot from China: Qwen, DeepSeek, and others. Suddenly researchers and startups could actually get their hands on competitive models, and that unlocked a huge amount of work on inference, fine-tuning, and serving. That's the part I've been closest to. Projects like vLLM and SGLang grew out of academic groups, and they grew fast because there was real demand: people had good models and needed to run them efficiently and cheaply.

The second change is who participates. It used to be mostly individual contributors and a few companies sponsoring maintainers. Now you have hardware vendors, cloud providers, and model labs all contributing to the same projects, because the serving layer became a shared piece of infrastructure that everyone depends on. That's healthy, but it also changes the dynamics. You have to think more about governance, about keeping the project neutral, and about not getting pulled in a direction that only benefits one sponsor.

The third thing is speed. The gap between a paper and a usable open implementation used to be months. Now it's sometimes days. A new attention variant or a new quantization method shows up, and someone has a pull request before the weekend. That's exciting, but it also means maintainers are under a lot more pressure, and burnout is a real issue that the community doesn't talk about enough.

So overall I'd say it's become more important, more competitive, and more professional. It's less of a hobbyist space and more like critical infrastructure. That's a good thing for users, but it means we have to be more deliberate about sustaining the people doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses new corporate and industry participation and governance concerns, but does not say that opportunistic participation weakens existing believers’ confidence in open source.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that sincere participants have difficulty distinguishing genuine commitment from participation for instrumental reasons.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest changes is that open source has become a much more collaborative process. People aren’t just releasing code; they’re sharing what they’ve learned, identifying problems, and building on one another’s work. That makes it easier for someone with a good idea to contribute, even without the resources of a large company.

At the same time, we have to distinguish between making something available and making it useful to the community. Can people understand it, reproduce the results, and adapt it to their own needs? Documentation, evaluation, and maintenance matter a lot, even though they don’t always receive as much attention as a new release.

So I’m optimistic about the growing participation, but I think the important question is how to sustain it. A healthy open-source community needs people who keep improving projects and supporting users over time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses growing participation and sustaining projects, but does not say that opportunistic participation weakens existing believers’ confidence in open source.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe difficulty distinguishing genuine commitment from participation driven by instrumental motives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest changes is that open source has become a much broader conversation. People aren’t just asking, “Is the code available?” They’re also asking, “Can I actually use it, modify it, and build on top of it?” In AI, that gets more complicated because the code, model weights, training data, and training process are different pieces, and releasing one doesn’t necessarily make the whole system open.

The community also plays a bigger role in shaping what happens after a release. People adapt models, find limitations, improve efficiency, and bring them into applications that the original developers might never have considered. So I see open source increasingly as a process of collaboration, rather than just the act of publishing something. The challenge is making that collaboration sustainable: keeping projects maintained, giving contributors credit, and making it easier for new people to participate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collaboration and sustainability, but does not say opportunistic participation weakens existing believers’ confidence in open source.

r002.rationale: The response does not address difficulty distinguishing genuine commitment from participation driven by instrumental motives.
